title: Rules, anomaly detectors and PU learning in the model screen
request: Compare the families the hand solution compared: percentile rules, anomaly detectors and positive-unlabelled learning next to the classifiers, on the same folds, and choose by a rule written before the screen.
spec: For binary rare-event tasks: a percentile rule score, unsupervised detectors (Isolation Forest, ECOD) fitted without labels and without resampling, and PU bagging; ranked on the same folds and metrics; the selection rule written in the record before the screen. Done when the screen lists every family, no resampler can precede a detector, and the choice cites the rule.
plan: Write expansion/detectors.py: PercentileRules, ECOD, an Isolation Forest detector and PUBagging, each with the classifier interface the runner uses.
Add them to the screen for a rare event only, and write the selection rule into the models record before the screen runs.
Test that detectors never see labels or resampled rows, and that the rule prefers a simpler family only within noise.
Fix the rule and the scope after the Step 2 review.

decisions.decision: Detectors are fitted on every fit row, never on labels and never after resampling.
decisions.why: An anomaly detector learns what normal looks like; labels or duplicated rare rows would turn it into a weak classifier.

decisions.decision: The rare families are a separate RARE_FAMILIES tuple that the engine adds only for a rare event.
decisions.why: Adding them to the general binary-imbalanced list changed every research campaign's screen and ranking.

decisions.decision: The rule: the best mean, then the simplest family within 10% of it whose paired gap stays within the one-sided t bound, never one the best beats on every fold, folds without a positive left out.
decisions.why: With three folds the t bound alone is so wide that a much weaker simple family wins; a practical margin and a never-beaten-everywhere check keep 'simpler' honest.

change: expansion/detectors.py (percentile rules, ECOD, Isolation Forest, PU bagging), runner.RARE_FAMILIES added by the engine for a rare event, the rare-event selection rule in the models record, the families' imports in the notebook export; tests in tests/test_core_behaviour.py and tests/test_labels.py.

findings.defect: When any fold had no positive, the rule always chose the first simple family.
findings.scenario: xgboost folds [0.80, 0.82, None] against percentile_rules [0.05, 0.04, None] chose percentile_rules: the None made the paired gain NaN, so 'adopted' was False and the first family in the simplicity order won. Folds without a positive do occur in the Home flow's tests.
findings.cause: Missing fold metrics entered the paired comparison.
findings.fix: Pair only folds where both values are finite, and keep the best when fewer than two remain.
findings.impact: Whenever one fold had no positive, which happens in the Home flow's tests and in rare-event data generally, the screen picked the first simple family regardless of scores, so a project could ship a percentile rule scoring 0.05 over a classifier scoring 0.80, with a record citing the rule as the reason.

findings.defect: The rule picked clearly weaker simple families.
findings.scenario: In the Home flow on the replica percentile_rules (mean AP 0.335) beat extra_trees (0.603), though extra_trees won all 3 folds (gain +0.27, bound 0.317); on acceptance seed 0 isolation_forest (0.505) beat pu_bagging (0.645).
findings.cause: With 3 folds the one-sided t bound (t about 1.89 with 2 degrees of freedom) is very wide, so 'within noise' covered large real gaps.
findings.fix: A simpler family must also be within 10% of the best's mean, and is never preferred when the best wins every fold.
findings.impact: A team would have been handed a percentile rule with mean AP 0.335 instead of extra trees at 0.603, a model that won every fold, because three folds make the noise bound so wide that almost any gap counts as noise.
findings.open: The screen still shows each family's mean and spread over folds, not bootstrap intervals.

findings.defect: The new families changed the research harness.
findings.scenario: Adding them to MODEL_FAMILIES['binary_imbalanced'] made every research campaign screen and rank them with the standard rule, and listed them for every binary project.
findings.cause: The engine-only addition was made in a list shared with the campaigns.
findings.fix: A separate RARE_FAMILIES tuple the engine adds only when the task is a rare event.
findings.impact: Every research campaign and every binary project would have started screening rules, detectors and PU bagging under the standard rule, changing the harness's results and runtime without a decision to do so.

findings.scenario: A project whose rule chose ecod raised KeyError 'ecod' in the notebook export, so the export route returned a 500 and the intern's capture failed.
findings.cause: MODEL_IMPORTS had no entry for the new families.
findings.fix: Add the four families' imports and constructors to the export.
findings.impact: Exporting any project whose screen chose one of the new families returned a server error, and the intern's capture failed with it, so the person lost their notebook for exactly the rare-event projects this package serves.
alternatives: Refuse the export with a 409 that says why: set aside because the four families can be written into the notebook directly.

outcome: Done: rules, ECOD, Isolation Forest and PU bagging screened for rare events only, detectors never on labels or resampled rows, chosen by a rule written before the screen. Open: the screen shows mean and spread, not bootstrap intervals; PU bagging is screened for complete labels too.
lessons: A preference for simplicity needs a practical margin, not only a significance bound, when there are only a few folds.
A missing fold score must be removed from a paired comparison, never allowed to turn the comparison into NaN.
Adding a family to a shared list changes every caller of that list.
risks: A selection rule that compares paired fold scores must handle folds with no positive, or a missing value decides the choice.
With very few folds a 'within noise' test admits large real gaps; preferring the simpler family needs a practical margin too.
Unsupervised detectors must be fitted without labels and never after a resampler, or they learn from the labels they claim not to use.
Families added for one task must not leak into the shared list the research campaigns screen.
Every family the screen can choose must be exportable to the notebook, or refused there with a reason.
